stages.title: Supply
stages.sub: Why firms supply more at higher prices, and what shifts the whole supply curve.

steps.q: To build a workable model, economists assume everyone weighs up costs and benefits sensibly, rather than acting randomly. If a bakery owner could sell bread for £5 or £2, which price would this sensible-weighing owner pick, all else equal?
steps.right: £5, the one that benefits them more
steps.hint: A sensible decision-maker compares the two prices and picks the one that leaves them better off.

steps.q: A bakery owner is assumed to weigh up costs and benefits sensibly. Of all the possible goals a bakery could chase, which is the one this assumption says the owner is aiming for?
steps.right: Making as much profit as possible
steps.wrong: Selling as much bread as possible
steps.hint: Profit, not just sales volume, is what makes the owner better off.

steps.q: A bakery aims to make as much profit as possible. If the price of bread rises, would a profit-seeking bakery want to offer more loaves for sale, or fewer?
steps.hint: More loaves sold at a higher price means more revenue for the same aim of maximising profit.

steps.q: Flour becomes cheaper to buy and nothing about the price of bread changes. Does the bakery's supply curve slide along itself, or move to a new position altogether?
steps.right: It moves to a new position altogether
steps.hint: The price of bread did not change, so the curve cannot be sliding along its own line.
